audits.claim: 752 is a fragmentary love letter whose text requests a reply and invokes divine judgment; the record offers translations including R. Kovalev and Jos Schaeken/Brill (2019) (entry lines 77, 79, 80).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (HTTP 200; both English translation blocks displayed)
audits.source_locator: metadata fields 'Сохранность', 'Категория', 'Жанр', 'Содержание'; Russian translation; English translations credited to R. Kovalev and to © Jos Schaeken / Brill Publishers, 2019
audits.source_excerpt: Сохранность: фрагмент … Жанр: частное письмо … Содержание: Любовное письмо; Kovalev: 'Write (answer) me about'; Schaeken: 'God will judge (you), and I will.'
audits.basis: Genre, fragmentary state, the reply request and a divine-judgment closing are all present, and both credited translations exist as the entry states. The two renderings do diverge at the close (Kovalev: 'God and my own wretchedness (i.e., I) will judge (you)'), so 'invokes divine judgment' is safe while the exact closing clause is translation-dependent.
audits.access_limit: Catalogue-level fields only; the print editions behind the two translations were not consulted.

audits.claim: Rock (2007) challenges the modern idea of an inherently half-pagan Russian Christianity and traces the nineteenth-century scholarly and Soviet histories of that interpretation (entry lines 108, 176).
audits.source_excerpt: This volume shows how the concept of dvoeverie arose with nineteenth-century scholars obsessed with the Russian 'folk' and was perpetuated as a propaganda tool in the Soviet period
audits.basis: The description also states that the book surveys eleventh-to-seventeenth-century uses of the term and concludes that 'double-belief' is a modern academic construct, matching the entry's 'contested explanatory model' calibration and its rule that a medieval accusation and a modern survival claim are different claims.
audits.access_limit: Publisher blurb and contents only; chapter-level arguments and the book's own treatment of Rod/rožanicy were not retrievable, so no page-level citation is claimed.

audits.claim: Chronicle annal 980 has Vladimir setting up images of Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh (entry line 94).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (15004361-byte PDF downloaded and converted locally with pdftotext -layout; 14029 extracted lines)
audits.source_locator: Cross and Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1953, annal 980, printed pp. 93-94 = extracted text lines 3936-3940
audits.source_excerpt: he set up idols on the hills outside the castle with the hall: one of Perun, made of wood with a head of silver and a mustache of gold, and others of Khors, Dazh'bog, Stribog, Simar'gl, and Mokosh'
audits.basis: All six names appear in the annal-980 princely cult passage, in the same order the entry lists them. The edition prints Dazh'bog and Simar'gl where the entry writes Dazhbog and Simargl - a transliteration difference, not a substantive one. The edition's own notes (extracted text line 9508 ff.) show the comparative conjectures the entry's line 194 warns against.

audits.claim: Vladimir Monomakh's Testament identifies a baptismal name Basil/Vasiliy alongside Vladimir, the Rus' name, and Monomakh as a byname; the entry cites Appendix I, p. 206 (entry line 161).
audits.source_locator: Appendix I 'The Testament of Vladimir Monomakh', ToC p. 206 = extracted text lines 8624-8628
audits.source_excerpt: I, wretched man that I am, by my pious and glorious grandsire Yaroslav named at baptism Basil (Vasiliy) and with the Russian name Vladimir, surnamed Monomakh by my beloved father and mother
audits.basis: Both the printed-page target (Appendix I begins at p. 206) and the three-name structure - baptismal Basil/Vasiliy, Rus' name Vladimir, byname Monomakh - check out. The passage is the Testament's own opening statement, consistent with the entry's caution that it concerns the later prince, not the tenth-century conversion narrative.
audits.access_limit: English translation used; the Laurentian text behind the translation was not consulted.

audits.claim: The label `nožnici` remains unidentified and must not be silently corrected to `rožanicy`, assigned to a deity or garment, or turned into a priesthood; no Rod/rožanicy-specific early ritual costume is established (entry lines 127-128; costume table row 134 'Scissors initiate a kinship rite'). This audit tests the language-myth-dress coupling rather than an isolated bibliography fact.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (two lexical records fetched: Slovak `nožnice`, Russian `ножницы`); attribution indexes returned zero hits for the term in a Rod/rožanicy context
audits.source_locator: Slovak entry `nožnice`, noun, plurale tantum, further reading citing Slovníkový portál Jazykovedného ústavu Ľ. Štúra SAV; Russian entry `ножницы`, etymology 'Образовано от сущ. нож'
audits.basis: The form coincides with ordinary Slavic nouns for scissors (Slovak nožnice, Polish nożyce, Lower Sorbian nožyce, Russian ножницы from нож), so a deity, priesthood or robe reading of the label has no lexical support and the implement reading is testable. However, no retrieved source attests the form in any Rod/rožanicy, homiletic or dress context, so the entry's unidentified status and its (to-verify) flags stand unchanged. A dated erratum recording this lexical reading and these limits was appended to the entry; no earlier bytes of the entry were rewritten. The ru.wikipedia search API returned totalhits 0 for 'ноужници'.
audits.access_limit: Crowd-edited dictionaries plus one national dictionary portal, consulted 2026-10-17; the Slovak claim is reported by Wiktionary citing the SAV portal, which was not fetched directly. Ivanits 1989 (lending-restricted) could not be searched for the term.

audits.claim: Cyril and Methodius's Moravian mission begins in 863; Glagolitic is associated with Constantine-Cyril's ninth-century work; early Cyrillic developed in the Bulgarian literary setting rather than being invented by Cyril personally (entry lines 27, 61, 66).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (encyclopedic tertiary source, not a scholarly monograph)
audits.source_locator: sections 'Mission to the Slavs: Great Moravia' and 'Invention of the Glagolitic and Cyrillic alphabets'; the latter quotes the papal letter Industriae tuae (880)
audits.source_excerpt: In 863 they began translating the Gospels … into what is now known as Old Church Slavonic … The early Cyrillic alphabet was developed by the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius at the Preslav Literary School
audits.basis: Both statements the entry relies on are present, and the article's quotation of Industriae tuae attributing the alphabet to 'Constantine the Philosopher' supports the entry's split between a Cyril-associated Glagolitic and a later, Bulgaria-based Cyrillic. This is tertiary support only; the entry's own shelf citations (Schenker 1995, Lunt 2001) were not retrieved for this layer.
audits.access_limit: Single encyclopedic source; Encyclopaedia Britannica returned HTTP 403 and the dated scholarly literature was not fetched, so the 863 anchor rests on tertiary agreement plus the entry's existing shelf.
